title: After AI Steals the Talent, Crypto's Only Opportunities Are Six Tokens
dek: Delphi's Yan Liberman says crypto VCs make only one deal a year because AI has sucked up all the smart people; the only ones that can actually make money are a handful of tokens with real revenue that don't depend on crypto market conditions.
why: A frontline crypto VC publicly shares his six holdings and his logic, including why he no longer does crypto VC and why he's given up on the gaming sector. High information density, but requires some crypto background.
who: Crypto fund managers, token investors, and practitioners who want to understand how frontline crypto VCs allocate capital and evaluate founders.
skip: The ad segment from 16:17 to 17:57 can be skipped.

points.h: This rally has no obvious buyers
points.body: Yan says the market was caught off guard by ‘QE in the form of long-end bond curve control’, triggering a short squeeze, but he personally finds it hard to see new highs in the short term because it requires a lot of new money, and the obvious buyer historically (Sailor) isn't buying now, instead cashmaxing and repaying preferred stock. He believes leverage hasn't over-accumulated, and this sequence of slow grind, pause, alt rotation is actually healthy. Another structural change is that the alt market has become shallower, making it easier for capital to concentrate in a few assets, so a whole new batch of buyers isn't needed to drive the market—this has become a ‘stock picker's market’.

points.h: Buy things that look like hot coins but are less crowded
points.body: Yan admits there are only about 10 to 15 investable liquid tokens right now, and all crypto funds are already allocated to these 15. His conclusion: you should look for targets that ‘look and smell like these coins, but aren't as crowded in trading’. Hyperliquid is a long-term bull, but rising to 200 in four months would be surprising; for short-term excess returns, you must look at less obvious names. Santi adds that with 15 investable coins, any liquid fund going on a show repeatedly names the same five.

points.h: Crypto VC does only one deal a year
points.body: Yan says of their latest VC fund's five investments, only one is crypto, and in the past year they did only one crypto VC deal. The reason is that crypto VC's value capture and defensibility are now clearer, allowing quick filtering of many projects, but the thesis that ‘crypto is being widely adopted across multiple verticals’ has been sidelined, and AI is a major factor in attracting talent, attention, and capital. His only crypto investment is Tori Finance, a tokenized Turkish lira arbitrage trade, USD-hedged, with about 10.5% organic yield and no incentives.

points.h: The six tokens share revenue not dependent on crypto
points.body: Yan's six publicly disclosed tokens are Hyperliquid, Zcash, Lighter, Venice, Grass, Aerodrome. He says he prefers projects with a ‘revenue story’ that aren't highly dependent on crypto activity, because they are more resilient and have a stronger TAM story. He detailed Grass: projected $70 million revenue, $40 million operating profit, doing residential IP network data scraping, clients are frontier labs, token market cap $330 million, unlock ends in October, about 30% of supply in the foundation, no equity only foundation, and if valued as a pure equity non-crypto business, the private market could probably raise $1 to 2 billion.

Yan says he no longer anchors on annualized returns, but sets individual price targets, stop losses, and invalidation conditions, and keeps a reserve for a ‘total collapse’ scenario. He admits he just likes volatility. Santi says he now doesn't do crypto VC that can't at least 10x, Ethereum at $300 billion market cap can't see a clean 10x, and the downside asymmetry is far greater than the upside. Yan responds that comfort comes from holding ‘productive assets’ rather than ‘reflexive assets’, and the key to productive assets is the durability of earnings and how much they depend on reflexive assets.

points.h: The gaming sector has been abandoned
points.body: Yan says gaming as a whole is a difficult vertical to invest in because the lifecycle of games as a business is too short, and when you run the NPV, the long-term value story is hard to justify. They tried Gunzilla, a big bet, and the result was not good; he attributes it to management and spending issues, not game quality—the game itself is AAA level, on par with Call of Duty, PUBG, Fortnite. He says this might be their last attempt at AAA level, and after that gaming as a broad category will be hard, with only small versions of games doing well. They now believe the only truly investable vertical is basically ‘financialized applications’.

points.h: Aerodrome is a typical catch-up trade
points.body: Yan says Aerodrome originally planned to migrate to mainnet in mid-July and support multi-chain, but it was delayed, hurting the price; now the release is set for the second half of September, with migration to ETH and ARC announced, and whether it migrates to Robin Hood is unconfirmed. He sees this as a huge opportunity for TVL, trading volume, and fees, and many treat it as a catch-up trade. The previous issue was the relationship between emissions and revenue—emissions to LPs, revenue to stakers, criticized as using emissions to offset revenue. Now they want to make emissions dynamic, tied one-to-one with trading volume, so price up emissions down; at the same time adding multiple revenue lines, estimated to contribute an additional 40% revenue with no emissions offset. Currently OI relative to market cap position is not much.

points.h: The investment committee now values founders most
points.body: Yan says if he could pick only one change, it's the weight of founder due diligence. In early crypto, it was obvious what needed to exist, so investing was more about ideas and defensibility, with lower founder weight. But entering other professional verticals, you can't really due diligence the idea and moat; the only repeatable, scalable thing is the founder side. They now ask ‘what is your earliest memory, and then take us through your life’. He also mentions childhood trauma bringing a ‘chip on the shoulder’ and a desperate desire to win as actually valuable factors, citing Athena's Guy as an example, saying he will stop at nothing to win.
